thread.title: How these major Charlotte employers are tackling mobile-app trends

author: Caroline Hudson
title: How these major Charlotte employers are tackling mobile-app trends
text: – Staff Writer, Charlotte Business Journal Jan 26, 2018, 8:41am EST For technology-related industries, the rise of the mobile app came naturally, but for legacy firms, the transition hasn’t been so simple. And the trend hasn’t shown signs of slowing down. As of 2016, there were about 4 billion smartphone systems installed worldwide. At a CIO Insight forum this week, panelists representing some of Charlotte’s largest employers talked about the decade-long life of the mobile app and how they are accommodating the trend. Arvy Rajasekaran , chief information officer at Detroit-based Ally Financial Inc. (NYSE: ALLY), says the online platform was vital to Ally’s foundation, having no brick-and-mortar branches like other traditional banks. Several years ago, the need for a mobile app for customers became apparent. Rajasekaran was one of four panelists at the CIO Insight forum Wednesday evening. Fellow panelists included: Steve Hagood , CIO at manufacturing company Ingersoll Rand Inc. (NYSE: IR); Chris Heck , CIO at Duke Energy Corp. (NYSE: DUK); and Egon Rinderer , head of the Global Technical Account Management Team at system-management company Tanium. “When we first launched it, speed was very important to us,” Rajasekaran says of Ally’s mobile app. “We went back and revisited, redid all the apps about four years ago, and then from that point on, the adoption has been really good.” Sixty percent of Ally customers use the mobile platform, Rajasekaran says. The U.S. ranks No. 4 globally in smartphones per capita, while South Korea holds the No. 1 spot. Although Android holds 80% of the global market share, Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL) is the choice for more than half of American smartphone users. Duke Energy has had a much different experience with the mobile app. Although the company developed a B2E (business-to-employee) platform for use, there is no customer-based app as of yet — a reality Heck views as “embarrassing.” Looking back, Heck says Duke Energy’s legacy systems should’ve been addressed years ago. However, the Charlotte-based company is piloting its first customer app now and plans to debut it in the second quarter. “The holdup has been legacy systems. Our legacy customer systems are 25-plus years old,” Heck says. “We’ve learned a lot in that 10-year span.” Employee apps at Duke Energy started in the nuclear department to promote efficiency and to cut down on the amount of paper used, Heck says. The technology has trickled down to other departments, and app/device distribution is now around 10,000 for 30,000 employees. “We actually had a funeral procession for the clipboard,” Heck says with a smile. “That was one milestone, but now it’s really process improvement. ... How can we transform the experience for the employee?” Ingersoll Rand, which has its operational headquarters in Davidson, delved into B2E apps for similar reasons, but it was by and large a cost-driven move, Hagood says. “The dynamic I’m starting to see, at least for us, is as the workforce gets a little younger and as we transition into the next generation of the workforce, there’s a little bit more of an expectation and a desire to do self-service,” he says. Similar to how employees are starting to drive app use, customers also drive the evolution of a company’s app architecture. At Ally, Rajasekaran says the digital platforms must be able to accommodate multiple channels with millions of customers logging on every day. “There’s a customer expectation, and so the way we approach it is really more about what are the features the customers are using? What channels are they using?” Rajasekaran says. These are the questions companies will likely ask more and more in the coming years. IHS Markit research says the smartphone install base is expected to reach 6 billion by 2020. The mobile app trend is here to stay — at least for now — and these Charlotte-area employers know digital innovation is a key to success. – Staff Writer, Charlotte Business Journal Jan 26, 2018, 8:41am EST Related Content
